topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European digital public health contexts; findings may have limited applicability to Australian healthcare systems, which have different regulatory frameworks, funding structures, and digital infrastructure priorities.
takeaways: Competency frameworks for digital health roles should address both technical skills and broader capabilities like change management and cross-functional collaboration — applicable when designing AI literacy programs for Australian health organisations.

European frameworks identify specific competency clusters (e.g. data literacy, systems thinking, regulatory knowledge) that can inform structured AI capability development pathways tailored to different health sector roles.

Consider how to adapt competency standards to Australia's healthcare context, as EU frameworks may reflect different regulatory requirements (e.g. GDPR) and workforce structures not directly transferable.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Likely limited to public health education contexts; applicability to other sectors and non-academic settings unclear without access to full methods.
takeaways: Faculty development programs that address resistance through structured learning pathways can shift academic staff from scepticism to active engagement with AI tools — consider designing similar change management approaches for your workplace AI adoption.

Public health educators face distinct barriers to AI literacy (domain-specific concerns, ethical considerations); assess whether your sector has comparable unique obstacles that require tailored rather than generic AI literacy interventions.

articles.title: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies - Sage Journals
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies  Sage Journals
articles.generalisability: Limited — the article focuses on Generation Z and educational strategies, but the geographic scope and specific educational contexts are not detailed in the snippet. Applicability to Australian educational settings and older workforce cohorts unclear.
takeaways: Identify specific AI literacy gaps in your Gen Z hires or teams to target upskilling interventions more effectively than broad training approaches.
Consider embedding AI capability development into formal onboarding and early-career development programs rather than treating it as a standalone module.
Map your organisation's evolving job roles and skill requirements over the next 3–5 years to align educational strategies with actual business needs.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; geographic scope and specificity of framework unclear from title and snippet alone. Findings may not directly transfer to adult workplace AI literacy programmes.
takeaways: Consider embedding AI competencies within a broader digital literacy framework rather than teaching AI in isolation — this holistic approach may improve retention and contextual understanding for learners of any age.

A structured digital literacy framework designed for younger learners could inform scaffolding strategies for adult employees new to AI, particularly around foundational concepts before moving to applied skills.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on higher education sector; applicability to organisational training contexts depends on whether recommendations transfer from academic to workplace settings.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most critical for your organisation (technical, ethical, domain-specific) and design curricula or training modules accordingly, rather than defaulting to one-size-fits-all approaches.

Consider layered competency development: foundational AI literacy for all employees, intermediate skills for roles interfacing with AI, and advanced expertise for specialists — mirroring higher education's differentiated pathway model.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education context; applicability to corporate workplace learning and AI capability development in non-academic sectors would require adaptation.
takeaways: Consider AI literacy as a foundational meta-skill that integrates technical knowledge, critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and organisational adaptability — useful for structuring multi-domain AI capability development programmes.

The four-domain model framework (likely spanning technical, cognitive, ethical, and organisational dimensions) can inform curriculum design for employee AI training, moving beyond technical skills alone to address change readiness.
Academic management innovation processes may offer transferable insights for how organisations can systematically embed AI literacy across leadership and staff cohorts.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — appears to be a single empirical study; generalisability depends on sample size, sector, and geographic scope, which are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Leaders can mitigate job insecurity fears triggered by AI adoption by demonstrating transformational leadership behaviours (vision, inspiration, individualized support), which may buffer anxiety and preserve morale during technological transitions.

Investing in employee self-efficacy training or coaching before and during AI implementation may reduce perceptions of job threat, as individuals with stronger confidence in their ability to adapt report lower job insecurity.

HR and leadership teams should treat job insecurity as a malleable outcome of AI adoption rather than inevitable; proactive culture-building around both leadership style and capability development can improve employee resilience.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability limited by focus on paternalistic leadership contexts, which are more prevalent in certain cultural settings (e.g., East Asia). Findings may not transfer directly to Western egalitarian or distributed leadership models common in Australia.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in customizing or configuring AI systems to fit their workflows — this sense of ownership appears to strengthen collaboration and engagement with AI.

In paternalistic or hierarchical organizational structures, leader involvement in 'AI crafting' (adapting AI to organizational needs) can validate and encourage employee participation, making AI adoption feel safer and more purposeful.

Consider whether your organization's leadership style aligns with the conditions that build AI ownership; teams under more collaborative or distributed leadership may need alternative strategies to achieve similar collaboration outcomes.

articles.title: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky. - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky.  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Conceptual rather than empirical — raises general concerns about employee AI use without specifying geographic scope or sector limitations. Likely reflects practices most developed in US and Western organisations with high AI adoption.
takeaways: Establish clear organisational policies on which AI tools employees can use for work-related tasks, specifying data confidentiality risks and approved alternatives for sensitive information.

Provide training to help employees distinguish between appropriate uses (e.g. drafting assistance, brainstorming) and risky uses of generative AI (e.g. sharing confidential client data, mental health disclosures, personal performance concerns).

Create psychologically safe channels for employees to discuss work stress and wellbeing concerns with managers or EAP services, rather than defaulting to AI chatbots that may not provide appropriate support.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title and snippet alone. The theoretical framework (Automation–Augmentation Paradox) is likely applicable across sectors, but geographic scope and sample composition require full article review.
takeaways: Generative AI adoption creates a paradox: it can either automate knowledge work (reducing employee engagement with learning) or augment it (deepening expertise). Managers should explicitly design AI implementation to favour augmentation by structuring tasks that require human judgment alongside AI assistance.

Monitor changes in employee knowledge-sharing behaviours after AI rollout—automation-focused implementations may inadvertently reduce collaborative learning and institutional knowledge retention. Consider whether knowledge behaviours have shifted from deep engagement to surface-level task completion.

articles.title: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear — snippet provides insufficient detail on sample size, geographic scope, sector, and methodology. Full article review needed to assess whether findings apply beyond the specific organisational or occupational context studied.
takeaways: Building AI self-efficacy among cybersecurity staff may buffer the negative effects of job stress on security behaviours — consider targeted training to strengthen confidence in AI-assisted security tasks.

Job stress appears to be a key barrier to safe cybersecurity practice in AI-enabled environments; assess stress levels and workload in your security teams as a first step to improving compliance and behaviour.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — full methodology needed to assess sample size, sector coverage, and geographic scope. The theoretical focus on psychological capital and AI as a job resource suggests potential applicability across algorithm-driven roles, but generalisability depends on study design and participant characteristics.
takeaways: Cultivate psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) in teams using AI tools — employees with higher PsyCap are better positioned to leverage AI as an enabler rather than threat, driving innovation outcomes.

When implementing AI systems, frame them as job resources that augment capability rather than replace workers — this framing can activate positive psychological states that support adaptation and creative problem-solving.

Assess and develop psychological capital alongside AI upskilling initiatives — traditional training alone may be insufficient if employees lack the psychological foundation (confidence, optimism, resilience) needed to engage innovatively with algorithmic tools.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford-based perspective without detail on empirical scope or geographic applicability. Findings and recommendations may reflect US higher education and tech sector biases.
takeaways: Identify specific work processes in your organisation where AI is already reshaping roles, then map skill gaps in your team to create targeted upskilling programs rather than broad, generic AI training.
Use this as a catalyst to run employee focus groups or surveys to understand anxieties about AI-driven job changes — addressing psychological safety concerns early prevents resistance to adoption.
Document concrete examples of how AI is changing job responsibilities in your sector, then co-design role transitions with affected staff to build buy-in and reduce change fatigue.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet alone. The approach-avoidance framework may apply broadly to AI adoption contexts, but geographic scope and sector representation are unclear.
takeaways: Use approach-avoidance theory to predict which employees will actively reshape their roles when AI is introduced — those motivated by opportunity (approach) will craft jobs toward AI collaboration, while those focused on threat mitigation (avoidance) will craft away from AI tasks.

Design AI adoption interventions that deliberately frame AI tools as opportunities rather than threats, since this mindset shift appears to influence whether employees proactively adapt their job duties or become passive resistors.

Monitor job crafting patterns during AI rollouts as an early indicator of successful adoption — employees who actively reconfigure their work (rather than retreating from AI-adjacent tasks) are likely to integrate AI more effectively into their roles.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reflects BCG's consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific examples and recommendations may be tailored to large enterprises with significant resources.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce transformation challenge requiring parallel investment in employee reskilling, role redesign, and change management — not just technology implementation.

Identify concrete workforce impact areas (specific roles, teams, processes affected) early and develop targeted upskilling pathways before widespread AI deployment to reduce disruption and resistance.

Establish clear communication about how AI will change day-to-day work and career progression; employees who understand their future role in an AI-enabled environment are more likely to engage with learning initiatives.

articles.title: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to Chinese primary and secondary school context. Findings may not generalise to other countries with different educational systems, teacher training approaches, or cultural attitudes toward technology adoption.
takeaways: AI adoption can paradoxically inhibit innovative teaching if teachers perceive it primarily as a threat to their autonomy or job security—assess and address teacher concerns about AI's role before implementation rather than assuming adoption alone drives behaviour change.

Frame AI tools as extending teacher agency (e.g., automating grading to free time for creative lesson design) rather than replacing expertise to shift perception from threat to challenge, which strengthens willingness to experiment with innovative practices.

Monitor psychological safety and perceived control over AI use; teachers who feel overwhelmed or disempowered are less likely to use AI creatively, so training and rollout should emphasise choice and gradual skill-building.

articles.title: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's methodology and sample composition, which are not detailed in the snippet. Findings may be limited by sector, organisational size, or geographic context not specified here.
takeaways: Implement DEI (Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion) interventions alongside AI adoption to mitigate algorithmic bias and ensure inclusive work design — generic DEI training alone is insufficient without deliberate algorithmic governance.

Build and reinforce diversity-supportive organisational culture as a moderating factor that enhances the effectiveness of AI systems; culture acts as a buffer against algorithmic discrimination when properly established before or during AI implementation.
Audit your current AI tools and work processes for bias, then pair technical fixes with targeted DEI initiatives and culture-building activities rather than treating these as separate workstreams.

articles.title: Reconfiguring work: Change management in the age of gen AI - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Reconfiguring work: Change management in the age of gen AI  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey research typically draws on global client work and surveys, but findings may reflect practices of large, well-resourced organisations and may not fully represent smaller firms or non-consulting sectors.
takeaways: Design change initiatives around specific AI use cases rather than broad 'digital transformation' to increase employee buy-in and demonstrate tangible value quickly.
Address role anxiety directly by mapping how AI will augment (not replace) existing jobs, then upskill employees in the new workflows before full implementation.
Establish cross-functional change teams that include frontline workers, not just leadership, to identify adoption barriers early and build grassroots support for the transition.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample size and composition, which are not detailed in the snippet provided. The findings likely apply broadly to memory and personality relationships, but specifics about participant demographics and study design are unclear.
takeaways: People with different personality types don't all remember surprising events the same way — some personalities appear to encode unexpected moments more vividly than others.
Your natural personality traits may influence which moments stick with you and which ones fade, suggesting surprise alone isn't the only ingredient for memorable experiences.
This hints at why eyewitness accounts of the same shocking event can vary so much between people — personality shapes what we encode, not just what actually happens.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Findings are preliminary and based on wine review analysis; generalisability to broader personality assessment depends on the validation methodology used, which is not detailed in the snippet.
takeaways: AI can detect personality traits from writing style in everyday contexts like wine reviews — suggesting our casual prose reveals more about us than we might realise.
Wine descriptions aren't just about flavour; they're a window into how differently people perceive and express the same experience based on their underlying personality.
The finding highlights how machine learning can uncover hidden patterns in human behaviour that traditional surveys might miss.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline-driven news summary of neuroimaging research; actual study details, sample size, and methodological rigour unknown from snippet alone.
takeaways: Brain imaging has detected structural or functional differences in people with psychopathic traits — suggesting personality disorders may have detectable biological signatures rather than being purely behavioural.

The finding is counterintuitive because psychopathy is often thought of as a purely behavioural or social condition, yet neuroscience keeps uncovering hard wiring differences that might explain why some people lack typical emotional responses.

This kind of research fascinates because it sits at the edge of nature vs. nurture — if brains are physically different, does that change how we think about accountability, treatment, or moral responsibility?

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to summarise a single study without details on sample size, geographic scope, or methodology; findings on personality traits may vary across cultural contexts.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissism (dominance-seeking, competitive behaviour) may paradoxically attract romantic partners despite its generally toxic reputation — challenging the assumption that only agreeable personalities succeed in dating.

The finding highlights a gap between what we think attracts people and what actually does; narcissistic traits associated with confidence and status-seeking can work in early-stage attraction, even if they often backfire later.

It's a reminder that human attraction is messily irrational — we're drawn to traits that might not make for great long-term partners, which explains why 'charismatic jerks' remain a persistent cultural archetype.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Moderate — suggests cross-cultural patterns in music–personality links, though actual sample composition and size not specified in snippet.
takeaways: Your taste in music might be a surprisingly reliable window into your personality — and this connection holds up across wildly different cultures, suggesting something universal about how people express themselves through sound.

The finding is counterintuitive because we often assume musical preferences are purely cultural or learned, yet personality-music links appear to transcend geography, hinting at deeper psychological or even biological foundations.
It's a fun reminder that despite our differences, humans everywhere seem to gravitate toward music that resonates with who they are — making your playlist a kind of global personality passport.

articles.title: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — news report format does not provide study details, sample size, or geographic scope. Generalisability depends on the underlying research not described in the snippet.
takeaways: A biological condition (hyperthyroidism) correlates with personality traits typically thought of as purely psychological — suggesting the mind-body connection is more intertwined than personality psychology usually assumes.
The finding is counterintuitive because we tend to think of 'dark' personality traits as stable psychological features, not something linked to a treatable medical condition.
If replicated, this could reshape how we think about personality: some traits we label as character flaws might partly reflect underlying physiological differences worth investigating.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified in snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings are specific to academic settings and multicultural team contexts. Generalisability to corporate or other organisational sectors unclear without access to full methodology. Geographic scope not specified in snippet.
takeaways: AI tools can be leveraged to support inclusive leadership practices that actively counteract gendered biases in team dynamics — consider piloting AI-assisted feedback or decision-support systems to flag potential gender disparities in meeting participation, credit attribution, or promotion pathways.

Multicultural teams may experience compounded visibility and inclusion challenges at the intersection of gender and cultural background — use psychological safety frameworks alongside AI tools to create explicit norms where all team members are heard, particularly those with intersecting minoritised identities.

Monitor whether AI-assisted interventions actually shift outcomes or simply create an illusion of inclusion — measure gendered participation, advancement, and belonging metrics before and after implementation to ensure algorithmic support translates to real cultural change.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: High — large global sample across multiple countries and sectors, though specific country-level breakdowns and sample composition details are not visible from the snippet alone. Results represent contemporary workforce sentiment but capture a single point in time.
takeaways: Identify which specific fears or hopes are most prevalent in your organisation by comparing PwC's global findings to your own employee engagement data — this gap analysis can reveal where psychological safety interventions are most needed.

Use survey insights about workforce concerns (likely including job security, AI impact, management trust) to inform listening sessions or focus groups with your teams, framing these as evidence-based rather than reactive.
Consider how PwC's global trends might differ in your Australian context — consult local employment relations data and cultural norms to adapt recommendations before implementation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to full article, geographic scope and sample characteristics cannot be assessed. Findings may not generalise across different cultural contexts, industries, or levels of AI implementation maturity.
takeaways: AI adoption can negatively impact employee wellbeing if it erodes psychological safety; leaders should proactively establish trust and open communication channels before and during AI implementation to mitigate depression and mental health risks.

Ethical leadership is a protective factor against adverse effects of AI adoption on mental health; invest in training managers to model ethical AI use, transparency about AI limitations, and fairness in decision-making to buffer employees against psychological harm.

Organisations should assess psychological safety climate as a key risk indicator when planning AI initiatives—monitor employee perceptions of safety to speak up about AI concerns, and address gaps before they compound into mental health issues.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Limited detail available from snippet alone; BCG reports typically draw on consulting engagements across multiple sectors and geographies, but the specific scope and sample characteristics cannot be determined from the title and snippet provided.
takeaways: Psychological safety creates more equitable participation — design team norms and leadership behaviours that explicitly invite contributions from quieter or marginalised voices, rather than assuming psychological safety emerges naturally.

Use psychological safety as a lever for inclusion outcomes — if your organisation is working on diversity or belonging initiatives, measure and track psychological safety as a concrete mechanism through which these initiatives create tangible change in who feels able to speak up.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — SHRM provides US-focused HR guidance; principles are broadly applicable but may not account for different regulatory contexts, cultural norms, or organisational structures in Australia.
takeaways: Identify the specific four leadership behaviours SHRM recommends and audit your current practice against each to identify which one requires most immediate attention in your team.

Psychological safety requires consistent demonstration — select one behaviour to focus on for the next month and track observable changes in team participation or idea-sharing before moving to the next.
SHRM's guidance is US-centric; adapt recommendations to Australian workplace culture, fair work obligations, and your organisation's existing policies around feedback and accountability.

articles.title: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — reflects practitioner observations likely from US/Western corporate contexts, but lacks empirical data on scope, sample size, or geographic applicability.
takeaways: Identify and address the specific fears driving non-transparency (e.g., job security concerns, fear of reprimand, uncertainty about policy) through confidential listening sessions or surveys before assuming employees will spontaneously disclose AI usage.

Establish clear, non-punitive policies on AI tool usage that explicitly separate compliance communication from performance evaluation — employees are more likely to be transparent when they're confident transparency won't be used against them.

Create safe disclosure channels (e.g., anonymous reporting, dedicated AI governance committees with employee representation) that signal the organisation values honest conversation about AI integration over surveillance or policing of tool adoption.
